questions.question: Follow one hundred units of insolation from the top of the atmosphere to the surface and back out, and explain why the budget balances for the planet as a whole yet global circulation is still necessary.
questions.expected_answer: Of one hundred units of incoming short-wave solar radiation, about thirty are reflected back to space by cloud tops, atmospheric dust and gases, and bright surfaces — the albedo. About twenty are absorbed on the way down, by ozone in the stratosphere and by water vapour, dust and cloud in the troposphere, since the atmosphere absorbs short-wave poorly. The remaining fifty are absorbed by the surface, which warms and re-radiates the energy as long-wave terrestrial radiation, because the earth is far cooler than the sun. The atmosphere absorbs long-wave well, so the outgoing energy is largely intercepted before finally being lost to space. Over a year the planet as a whole loses exactly what it gains, so the global budget balances. But latitudes within about forty degrees of the equator receive more than they lose — a permanent surplus — while higher latitudes lose more than they receive — a permanent deficit. Radiation cannot correct this locally, so winds and ocean currents such as the Agulhas transfer surplus heat poleward; global circulation exists to settle that imbalance.

questions.question: Set out the greenhouse mechanism in its five-step order, then explain the difference between the natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced greenhouse effect, naming three human sources of the latter.
questions.expected_answer: Step one: short-wave solar radiation passes through the atmosphere with little absorption. Step two: the earth's surface absorbs it and warms. Step three: the warm surface re-emits the energy as long-wave terrestrial radiation. Step four: greenhouse gases — water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone and CFCs — absorb that long-wave radiation. Step five: they re-radiate it in all directions, and the downward share, counter-radiation, warms the lower atmosphere. The natural greenhouse effect is essential: without it the global average would be about minus eighteen degrees instead of about fifteen. The enhanced greenhouse effect is the human intensification of the same mechanism — greenhouse gases added faster than natural sinks remove them. Three sources from: burning coal, oil and gas for electricity, industry and transport; deforestation, which removes a carbon sink and releases stored carbon; livestock and flooded paddies releasing methane; landfill decay; and cement manufacture. The natural effect keeps the planet habitable; the enhanced effect drives the warming, drought and food-security consequences facing Africa.

questions.question: Compare East London and De Aar using at least four temperature factors, and explain why their annual temperature ranges differ so sharply.
questions.expected_answer: Distance from the sea: East London sits on the coast, where the slow-heating, slow-cooling ocean cushions temperatures, while De Aar lies deep in the interior with no water body to steady it, so it bakes in summer and frosts in winter. Ocean currents: East London's shore is washed by the warm Agulhas Current, which warms and moistens the air, lifting winter temperatures and feeding summer rainfall; De Aar receives no such marine influence. Altitude: De Aar stands high on the interior plateau, losing roughly 6,5 degrees for every 1 000 metres, which deepens its winter cold, while East London is at sea level. Cloud cover: the moist coastal air over East London carries more cloud, which trims daytime maxima and holds up night minima, whereas De Aar's clear, dry skies allow scorching days and rapid night-time heat loss. Latitude is broadly comparable and so contributes little to the contrast. The result is a small annual range at East London — a maritime climate — against a large annual range at De Aar, the classic mark of continentality reinforced by altitude and clear skies.
